nodes.name: Find in Odoo
nodes.notes:
Waited on, unlike every other sub-workflow call in this system - the answer is
needed before the next decision can be made. Bounded by LP-90's own retry budget
(3 tries, 8s cap), so it cannot hang this execution indefinitely.

nodes.name: Read Person Index
nodes.notes:
anyCondition, so either identifier finds the person - the same human reaching us
by email one week and WhatsApp the next has only one of the two in common.

The __no_email__ / __no_phone__ sentinels are load-bearing. An empty string would
become `email_norm = ""`, which MATCHES EVERY WhatsApp-sourced row (they all have
no email) and would merge unrelated people into one another. A sentinel that
cannot occur in real data matches nothing, which is the intended meaning of
"I have no email to search on".

nodes.name: Read Stage Map
nodes.notes:
Fetched every run rather than cached. One extra round trip per lead buys the
guarantee that a stage added or renamed in Odoo this morning is honoured this
afternoon - no cache to invalidate and no "why did it go to the wrong column"
to debug. Caching it in lp_config with a TTL is the named optimisation if lead
volume ever makes the call worth removing.

nodes.name: Count Open Leads
nodes.notes:
Workload is COUNTED here, not kept as a running total on the agent row.

A stored counter has to be decremented on every path that ends an assignment -
closed, merged, opted out, reassigned by the tick, rejected by a manager - and
the first path anyone forgets leaves that salesperson permanently "full". The
seeded counters were in fact all still 0 after a full edge-case run, so
load-balancing was sorting by a column that never moved and every lead landed
on the same rep.

Counting live rows costs one extra read per lead and cannot drift. The trade is
the 250-row page ceiling; see Known Limitations for the point where a stored
counter becomes the right answer again.

nodes.name: Assign Owner
nodes.notes:
Rung 3 (nobody available or nobody with headroom) does NOT drop the lead. It goes
to the configured fallback owner and raises an alert, because an unassigned lead
is a lead nobody is accountable for - the failure mode this rung exists to
prevent. The tick in LP-04 reassigns it when capacity frees up. (EC-9)

nodes.name: Claim Odoo Upsert
nodes.notes:
Written BEFORE the CRM call, deliberately. A crash between this node and the next
leaves a row saying "someone started writing this lead to Odoo and never said it
finished" - which is a fact the reconciler can act on. Claiming afterwards would
leave no trace at all, and the lead would look untouched while an opportunity sat
in the CRM.

nodes.name: Odoo Upsert
nodes.notes:
Every input reads from Build Odoo Write by name rather than from $json, because
$json here is the row the claim node returned. Referencing the source node makes
the chain order explicit and removes any dependence on what a Data Table write
happens to emit.

nodes.name: Complete Claim
nodes.notes:
result_ref is the Odoo id. That single field is what makes a later replay able to
say "already done, here is the record" instead of writing a second opportunity.

nodes.name: Update Lead Record
nodes.notes:
Every column is mapped, not just the changed ones. The Data Table node has no
partial update - an upsert rewrites the whole row - so omitting a field blanks it.
That is a real limitation of the free built-in store and it is listed as such in
the design doc; on Postgres this would be an UPDATE ... SET of four columns.

nodes.name: Register Person
nodes.notes:
The index points at the SURVIVING lead, so the next enquiry from this person
resolves straight to the record that is actually being worked rather than to a
merged-away one.

nodes.name: Post Odoo Note
nodes.notes:
The audit trail a salesperson will actually read. Our lp_audit table is for
operators; this puts the score, the reason, the owner and the duplicate decision
in the chatter of the record itself, where the person working the deal is already
looking. Not waited on - a missing note must never fail a lead.

value.detail_json: ={{ JSON.stringify({ band: $json.band, stage: $json.stage_name, stage_event: $json.stage_event, closed: $json.close, duplicate: { action: $json.dup_action, reason: $json.dup_reason, candidates: $json.dup_candidates }, owner: { id: $json.owner_id, rung: $json.assign_rung, why: $json.assign_reason, alert: $json.assign_alert, load: $json.owner_load, team: $json.team_load }, recovery: $json.recovery, outreach: $json.outreach }) }}

nodes.name: Write Jobs
nodes.notes:
Upsert on a deterministic job_id (lead + cadence + step), so re-running this
workflow reschedules the same three jobs instead of queueing three more. Without
that, one replay would double every follow-up the lead receives.

value.context_json: ={{ JSON.stringify({ lead: $json.lead, score: $json.v.score, band: $json.band, owner_name: $json.owner_name, owner_email: $json.owner_email, odoo_lead_id: $json.odoo_lead_id, missing: $json.lead.validation_missing, dup_reason: $json.dup_reason, base_url: $json.cfg.base_url }) }}

parameters.content:
## LP-03 Route and Sync

**The only workflow with side effects.** LP-02 decided; this one writes to Odoo, assigns an owner, schedules follow-ups and sends the message. One writer per fact.

**Search before create, every time** - against Odoo, not just our index, and with `active_test:false` so a previously *lost* opportunity is visible. Without it, a lead the team already rejected gets recreated as new. **(EC-1, EC-2)**

**Claim -> write -> complete.** The ledger row goes in *before* the Odoo call, so a crash between them leaves evidence. `claimed` + a record found by external key = the write landed and the acknowledgement did not, and it is repaired instead of duplicated. **(EC-7)**

**Lost is not a stage** in Odoo - it is `active=false` + `probability=0` + a reason.

**Follow-ups are queue rows, not Wait nodes**, so an opt-out can cancel one. **(EC-10)**
